title: Daybook: inference sketches + reading notes (Amelia Choi)
content:
Quick framing / why I care:
- Want a compact set of heuristics (cheap compute + predictable latency) we can try for multi-session web chat and long-form summarization flows.
- Focus: KV cache eviction/summarization, prompt window stitching, and tiny evals that correlate with downstream UX.

Immediate takeaways from NeurIPS workshop skim (notes, not polished):
- Paper A (sparse-kv-2025): straightforward gains for persona-style sessions when you cluster keys by semantic chunking instead of recency. Empirically reduces cache churn for conversational agents.
- Paper B (longform-distill): distillation into chunked prefix LM works surprisingly well for extractive tasks; but hallucination risk grows if distillation clips are too short.
- Tooling idea from panel: always track token-level alignment error between cached prefix expansion and freshly computed continuations — simple metric but good signal for evictions.

Short summaries (paper-first-pass):
1) "Sparse semantic KV for conversational LMs" (arXiv 2025)
   - Core: replace naive recency LRU with embedding-cluster eviction. Keep a small per-session budget but allow grouping keys by cluster centroid and TTL.
   - Why it matters: for long-lived sessions (100s-1k tokens), improves relevant retrieval and keeps GPU KV cache small.
   - Caveats: embedding compute overhead; need fast incremental cluster updates.

2) "Distill-chaining for long context"
   - Core: distill intermediate chunks into compact prefixes that the model can condition on later. Distillation model targets extractive recollection.
   - Observed failure modes: loss of generative creativity; prompt leakage when distilled prefix encodes instructions too literally.

3) "Practical metrics for cache health" (workshop handout)
   - Proposed metrics: prefix-fidelity (KL or next-token match over small probes), cache-hit precision (how often cached prefix contributed to factual recall), eviction regret (downstream performance drop when evicted keys would have helped).

Notes-to-self / small experiments to run (prioritized):
A) Embedding-cluster eviction micro-experiment (2 days)
   - Dataset: 1k synthetic sessions from support chat logs (anonymized)
   - Implementation sketch: incremental k-means with k=8 clusters per session, update when new messages > 32 tokens. Evict oldest cluster when budget exceeded.
   - Metrics: pct cache hits, average latency, probe fidelity (sample 50 queries).
   - Risk: embedding cost -> precompute via light-weight encoder (distil-BERT-ish) + quantize.

B) Distill-as-prefix ablation (3 days)
   - Take long docs (wiki pages) and distill every 512 tokens into 64-token prefix using small finetune. Compare: no-distill vs distill-then-serve. Measure ROUGE / factual recall and hallucination probes.

C) Prefix-fidelity probe harness (1 day)
   - Simple: sample prompts that are sensitive to last 128 tokens, then measure probability mass assigned by model when using cached prefix vs full recompute. Report KL and top-1 match.

Implementation notes / engineering constraints:
- We need an async path for embedding updates: don't block token-serving. Queue updates, apply eventually consistent cluster changes.
- For Dedicated customers, exposing cluster budget and eviction policy as config knobs (policy: lru|semantic-cluster|ttllike) would be a nice quick win.
- Cache serialization: use compact int8 quantized tensors + cluster membership metadata (small). Consider existing proto format in runtime PR #345.

Open questions / research doubts:
- How correlated is prefix-fidelity (KL) with real-world UX metrics (user satisfaction, correction rate)? Hypothesis: moderate correlation but needs user-level evals.
- Distillation tradeoff: Can we learn small prefixes that preserve both extractive recall and generative style (maybe two-headed objective)?
- How to avoid prompt leakage when distilled prefixes accidentally encode instructions or private data? Need filters + redaction steps.

Links & quick refs I want to re-read:
- Sparse KV cluster idea: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.00001 (note: their code uses faiss + rebalanced TTL)
- Distillation chain methods: link from NeurIPS proceedings (saved PDF in personal folder)
- Runtime PR that touches KV serialization: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/345
- Slack thread: #inference-kv (pin-> "semantic-eviction-threads")

Quick heuristics cheat-sheet to test (for experiments):
- If session length < 300 tokens: no cluster eviction, pure LRU.
- If session length 300-1500 tokens: cluster-k=6, budget 128 keys.
- If session length >1500 tokens: enable distill checkpoints every 1024 tokens.

Notes for a tiny user test (playlab):
- Recruit 5 product testers, give them a long conversation scenario (support + follow-up). Flip between: no-cache, lru-cache, semantic-cluster. Use within-subjects design. Measure time to find previous fact, perceived helpfulness (1-5), and mistakes.

To-do (short):
- [ ] Hook up small encoder to runtime PR (Jonas?)
- [ ] Prototype cluster eviction in Python harness (use faiss or scikit-kmeans)
- [ ] Write lightweight eval harness for prefix-fidelity (1 pager)
- [ ] Draft short blurb for weekly sync (what we tested and immediate results)

Random scribbles / heuristics I keep returning to:
- "Eviction regret" sounds niche but product folks get it. Frame experiments around reducing regret with constrained budget.
- Cost policy: always show per-1000 token marginal cost for distillation step; otherwise product will balk.

End-of-day action: push a tiny branch that logs cache-hit precision for a couple hundred sessions; get initial signal.

2025-07-10 16:42 - flagged runtime PR #345 for cache serialization changes (Slack ping to Jonas)
2025-07-15 11:22 - first micro-harness run: naive cluster implementation, preliminary lower eviction churn (~+12% helpful hits) but embedding cost non-trivial
2026-02-03 10:05 - added NeurIPS panel notes and prioritized prefix-fidelity probe

——
Notes to self: keep this messy. Move the things that worked into a proper RFC when we have 1-2 reproducible evals.
